post.contentHtml:
Why the Stock Collapsed Despite Record Results

Japanese character company Sanrio (8136) plunged about 18% in a single day on the Tokyo Stock Exchange right after its August quarterly earnings release, even though both revenue and operating profit were the highest ever for a first quarter (April–June). This article looks at "why did the stock fall on good results?" and "is the strategy of reducing reliance on Hello Kitty working?"

Where the Stock Stands Now

  • October 9 close: ¥1,237 (about +2.9% from the previous day)
  • October 14 intraday price: around ¥1,280. However, the reliability of figures on some quote pages is low, so please treat this as a reference only.
  • This year's high: ¥1,470 (August 10, just before the earnings release) / this year's low: about ¥819 (May 7)
  • Based on the data provided, the 1-year price change is about -16.8%, and the dividend is ¥16.

In other words, the stock has risen sharply from its May low, but it is trading about 13% below the peak just before the earnings release.

August Q1 Results: Good Numbers, But...

ItemApril–June 2026Notes
RevenueAbout ¥52.0 billion+20.7% YoY, record for a first quarter
Operating profitAbout ¥22.4 billion+11.1% YoY, record for a first quarter
Market expectation for operating profit (consensus)About ¥23.4 billionActual figure fell short of expectations

Consensus means the average forecast of securities analysts. Operating profit fell slightly short of this expectation, and because the stock had risen about 55% since June, profit-taking sell orders poured in all at once. Morningstar assessed that results were broadly in line with its own estimates and that the share price had already reached a fair-value level.

The Key Issue: Overseas Costs

  • North America operating profit fell about 20% due to higher marketing expenses (while revenue rose 11.5%).
  • Asia operating profit fell about 5% due to higher selling, general and administrative expenses.
  • The company is also still absorbing the impact of US tariffs.

Sales volume overseas is growing, but spending is rising along with it, so profit growth is not keeping pace with revenue growth. This is exactly the point the market reacted to most sensitively.

Reducing Dependence on Hello Kitty

Hello Kitty's share of consolidated revenue has reportedly fallen to about 37%, and Sanrio is said to be growing other characters such as Kuromi and Cinnamoroll. When revenue is concentrated in one character, the blow is large when the trend fades; Sanrio's licensing-centered business model (earning fees by lending out the right to use characters) is now being combined with a more diversified character portfolio. A first game launch is also reportedly planned for this October. However, Morningstar believes the game will not become a meaningful profit driver in the short term.

This Year's Targets and Remaining Variables

  • The company maintained its guidance (annual targets set by the company) for the fiscal year ending March 2027: revenue of about ¥229.8 billion (+18.4%) and operating profit of about ¥89.5 billion (+15%).
  • First-quarter progress is about 22.6% of the revenue target and about 25% of the operating profit target, which the company says is in line with its internal plan.
  • Operating profit for the previous fiscal year (ended March 2026) rose about 50% to about ¥77.8 billion, but the filing of its financial results was delayed over an issue in which about ¥250 million in improper compensation was paid to a former executive at a US subsidiary, and governance improvements are under way.

Points to Watch

  • How the North American marketing cost burden shows up in margins in the second-quarter results around November
  • Trends in the revenue share of non-Hello Kitty characters such as Kuromi and Cinnamoroll
  • Reception after the first game's launch and its contribution to licensing revenue
  • Follow-up measures on governance improvements

In sum, rather than growth itself having stalled, Sanrio appears to be at a stage where heightened expectations after a sharp rally are colliding with the costs of overseas expansion. This is purely an interpretation based on publicly available figures, and the future direction of the share price cannot be known.

This article is not investment advice, and responsibility for investment decisions rests with the investor.
